CONFIDENTIAL LEGAL MEMORANDUM

RE: RED-FLAGS REPORT – PRAIRIE AEROSTRUCTURES HOLDINGS DILIGENCE REVIEW

DATE: [Current Date]
PREPARED FOR: [Client Name]

---

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

This red-flags report identifies key issues and areas of concern arising from the diligence review of Prairie Aerostructures Holdings (the "Company"). The analysis focuses on representations, warranties, covenants, conditions precedent, indemnification, and termination provisions in the operative transaction agreement, cross-referenced against firm precedent and market practice in aerospace vertical integration transactions.

---

CRITICAL RED FLAGS

1. REPRESENTATIONS AND WARRANTIES SCOPE

Flag: Breadth of Reps & Warranties Limitations
– Many aerospace sector acquisitions contain heavily carved-out representations, particularly regarding environmental compliance, product liability, and regulatory approvals. Standard market practice requires unqualified reps on core business operations and financial statements.
– ACTION REQUIRED: Verify that the Company's representations on (i) absence of undisclosed liabilities, (ii) compliance with FAA/ITAR regulations, and (iii) product quality certifications are not subject to "knowledge" qualifiers or materiality thresholds that would impair enforceability.

Flag: Survival and Basket Thresholds
– Aerospace transactions typically provide extended survival periods (18–24 months) for operational reps and longer for environmental/compliance matters. Short survival windows create indemnification risk.
– ACTION REQUIRED: Confirm survival periods meet market standards and that any "basket" (minimum claim threshold) does not exceed 0.25–0.50% of transaction value for fundamental reps.

---

2. REGULATORY & COMPLIANCE RISKS

Flag: ITAR/EAR Controls and Export Classification
– Prairie Aerostructures likely manufactures components subject to International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR) or Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Breach of these controls creates criminal and civil liability, and loss of facility security clearance.
– ACTION REQUIRED: Obtain representations that (i) facility maintains current ITAR registration/facility security clearance, (ii) all export classifications have been timely obtained, (iii) no denied parties or foreign ownership restrictions exist, and (iv) no prior violations or audit findings remain unresolved.

Flag: FAA Compliance and Product Certification
– Aerospace manufacturers must maintain FAA Parts Manufacturer Approval (PMA) or Design Approval (DA) certifications. Lapses or pending compliance issues directly impact revenue-generating capacity.
– ACTION REQUIRED: Verify current FAA certifications, airworthiness approvals, and technical data packages; confirm no outstanding corrective action notices (CANs) or audit findings.

Flag: Environmental Liability and Remediation
– Aerospace manufacturing involves hazardous materials (composite resins, coatings, solvents). Historical contamination and ongoing remediation costs may not be fully disclosed.
– ACTION REQUIRED: Obtain Phase I/II environmental assessments and representations that no environmental liens, pending agency actions, or undisclosed contamination exists; confirm materiality threshold for environmental reps.

---

3. FINANCIAL & OPERATIONAL RISKS

Flag: Working Capital and Inventory Valuation
– Aerospace supply chains are capital-intensive. Significant write-downs of slow-moving or obsolete inventory are common post-closing discoveries.
– ACTION REQUIRED: Verify that inventory reserve calculations align with historical obsolescence rates and current demand forecasts; obtain rep that inventory is valued at lower of cost or market.

Flag: Revenue Recognition and Customer Concentration
– Long-term fixed-price contracts in aerospace create margin pressure. Customer concentration above 10–15% of revenue introduces revenue volatility.
– ACTION REQUIRED: Obtain detailed customer concentration analysis, confirm top 5 customers represent sustainable demand, and verify no customer termination rights or renegotiation clauses triggered by change of control.

Flag: Supply Chain Dependencies
– Aerospace manufacturers depend on critical suppliers for specialized components. Single-source suppliers and long lead times create operational risk.
– ACTION REQUIRED: Map critical suppliers, confirm supply agreements survive change of control, and verify no material supplier termination or renegotiation rights triggered by transaction.

---

4. INDEMNIFICATION & ESCROW STRUCTURES

Flag: Indemnification Caps and Thresholds
– Caps should be calibrated to transaction value: 15–18% for general reps, 25%+ for fundamental reps (typically uncapped for tax/ITAR). Low caps expose buyer to uncovered losses.
– ACTION REQUIRED: Confirm indemnification cap structure aligns with aerospace market standards and that fundamental reps (regulatory compliance, title to assets, absence of material litigation) are uncapped or high-capped.

Flag: Escrow Period and Release Mechanics
– Shorter escrow periods (12 months) in aerospace transactions are disfavored due to the extended discovery timeline for latent defects and compliance issues.
– ACTION REQUIRED: Ensure escrow period is 18–24 months minimum and that indemnification claims are not time-barred prior to escrow release.

Flag: Earn-Out Provisions
– Earn-outs create ongoing disputes over revenue adjustments, working capital, and earn-out targets. These are particularly problematic if revenue is contingent on government contracts.
– ACTION REQUIRED: If earn-out exists, confirm clear definitions of revenue, validated third-party measurement, and materiality thresholds; confirm earn-out does not depend on regulatory approvals outside seller's control.

---

5. CONDITIONS PRECEDENT & CLOSING RISKS

Flag: Regulatory Approval Conditions
– FAA and export license approvals are often condition precedents. Undefined timelines or allocation of remediation costs create closing risk.
– ACTION REQUIRED: Confirm (i) outside date for regulatory approvals (typically 6–9 months), (ii) allocation of remediation costs (who bears cost of corrective actions), and (iii) buyer's walk-away rights if approvals are denied.

Flag: Change of Control Consents
– Major customers and suppliers often require change of control consent. Failure to obtain consents can result in contract termination and revenue loss.
– ACTION REQUIRED: Identify all contracts requiring consent; confirm seller has obtained or agreed to obtain consents pre-closing; if any material consents are outstanding, establish closing conditions and remedies.

Flag: Material Adverse Change (MAC) Definition
– MAC clauses must be specific and not overly broad. Aerospace-specific MACs should address FAA/ITAR compliance loss, customer concentration, and supply chain disruption.
– ACTION REQUIRED: Confirm MAC clause includes aerospace-specific triggers (regulatory license loss, major customer loss >15% revenue, supply chain disruption) and excludes general economic conditions, industry-wide events, and actions required by transaction.

---

6. TERMINATION & REMEDIES

Flag: Termination Rights and Reverse Termination Fees
– Reverse termination fees (if any) should be appropriate to transaction risk and exclude financing conditions if deal has adequate financing certainty.
– ACTION REQUIRED: If reverse termination fee exists, confirm it is capped at 3–4% of enterprise value and excludes financing-related termination rights.

Flag: Specific Performance Availability
– Aerospace transactions may be difficult to specifically perform if regulatory approvals are withheld. Clarify whether specific performance is available and under what conditions.
– ACTION REQUIRED: Confirm whether specific performance is available and under what conditions; if not, ensure monetary damages and walk-away rights are clearly defined.

---

7. TRANSACTION-SPECIFIC CONSIDERATIONS

Flag: Aerospace Vertical Integration Risks
– Vertical integration transactions (e.g., acquiring a supplier) create additional risks: supplier dependency on parent revenue, transfer pricing, allocation of overhead, and potential customer conflict concerns.
– ACTION REQUIRED: If Prairie Aerostructures is a supplier, obtain reps on (i) no exclusive supply relationships that may be terminated post-acquisition, (ii) no parent company dependency, (iii) capacity to serve external customers, and (iv) no customer conflicts with buyer's existing business.

Flag: Intellectual Property and Trade Secrets
– Aerospace design and manufacturing processes rely on proprietary technology. IP ownership and licensing issues can impair buyer's ability to operate the business.
– ACTION REQUIRED: Conduct IP due diligence; confirm (i) all proprietary manufacturing processes are owned by the Company, (ii) no third-party licenses restrict buyer's operations, (iii) no infringement claims or indemnification obligations from third parties exist, and (iv) trade secret protection measures are adequate.

Flag: Warranty and Indemnification Obligations to End Customers
– Aerospace components often come with extended warranties and indemnification for product defects. Undisclosed warranty claims and latent defects can create material post-closing liabilities.
– ACTION REQUIRED: Obtain detailed summary of all product warranties, pending warranty claims, and historical warranty claim costs; confirm seller indemnifies buyer for pre-closing defects and claims.

---

SUMMARY OF RECOMMENDED ACTIONS

1. Obtain unqualified representations on FAA/ITAR compliance and regulatory status; confirm no "knowledge" or materiality qualifiers.
2. Verify environmental assessments and confirm no undisclosed contamination or remediation obligations.
3. Validate customer concentration, revenue quality, and no change-of-control termination rights on material contracts.
4. Confirm critical supplier agreements survive change of control.
5. Ensure indemnification cap and escrow structures align with aerospace market practice.
6. Obtain all material regulatory consents pre-closing or establish closing conditions/remedies.
7. Conduct detailed IP due diligence and confirm no infringement or licensing restrictions.
8. Obtain detailed product warranty and warranty claim history; confirm seller indemnification.
9. Clarify MAC clause definition and confirm inclusion of aerospace-specific triggers.
10. If earn-out or reverse termination fee exists, confirm appropriate caps and clear measurement metrics.

---

CONCLUSION

The Prairie Aerostructures Holdings transaction presents the typical risk profile of an aerospace manufacturing acquisition, with particular focus on regulatory compliance, customer/supplier relationships, and product quality. Careful attention to representation scope, survival periods, indemnification structures, and closing conditions will be essential to mitigate post-closing liability and operational disruption.

This report should be reviewed in conjunction with the operative transaction agreement and updated as additional diligence materials become available.

---
